--    8  S2  promised 07 Mar  receipt 08 Mar   ordered  70  received  70
--    9  S2  promised 09 Mar  receipt 09 Mar   ordered  80  received  80
--   10  S2  promised 12 Mar  receipt open     ordered  30  received   0
-- Due lines (promised date before 10 March): 7. On time: 4. OTD = 4 / 7 = 57.1%.
--   S1: due 3, on time 1 = 33.3%;  S2: due 4, on time 3 = 75.0%.
--   OTIF = 3 / 7 = 42.9% (line 6 was on time but only 150 of 200 arrived).
-- Boundary cases on purpose: line 4 is promised today and open, so it is not due yet; line 5 arrived early for a March 20 promise and is not counted;
--   line 9 arrived on its promised day and is on time (receipt <= promised); line 3 is open and overdue and counts as late; line 8 is one day late.
-- With OTD Tolerance Days = 1: 5 due lines (lines 3 and 9 are promised 9 March, plus one day is 10 March, which is not before the as-of date, so both drop out), 4 on time
--   (line 8 now counts as on time). OTD = 4 / 5 = 80.0%.
-- Open and overdue with tolerance 0: line 3 only.

-- ==== How to adapt ====
-- Customer OTD: the same pattern on sales order lines (PromisedDate becomes the confirmed delivery date, ReceiptDate the ship or delivery date).
-- Different agreements per supplier: put the tolerance on 'Dim Supplier' and use MAX or SELECTEDVALUE of it inside a row-level FILTER with RELATED.
-- Month-end snapshots: replace the As Of Date measure by a fixed date so that the figure does not change when the report is opened later.
-- Weighted by value: replace COUNTROWS by SUMX of line value; report both counts and value, they tell different stories.
-- Show late days: add a measure with AVERAGEX over late lines of (ReceiptDate - PromisedDate), and treat open lines separately.

-- ==== Performance notes ====
-- FILTER over the fact table inside CALCULATE is evaluated for the rows in the current selection; for tens of millions of lines add a
--   calculated column [IsDue] and [IsOnTime] at refresh time, at the price of a fixed tolerance.
-- Keep PromisedDate and ReceiptDate as date type, not datetime, for compression and to avoid time-of-day errors.

-- ==== Common mistakes ====
-- Counting not-yet-due lines in the denominator (open lines lower OTD) or only early lines in the numerator (OTD above reality).
-- Using < where the agreement says 'on or before': a delivery on the promised day then counts as late.
-- Putting a measure inside a Boolean CALCULATE filter; use a variable.
-- Using ReceiptDate on the active relationship to Dim Date: the report period then moves lines between months when they arrive.
-- Averaging supplier OTD percentages in the total row; use the counts.
-- Ignoring partial deliveries and unit differences when you report OTIF.

-- ==== Privacy and safety ====
-- Supplier performance data is business data. Individual buyers should not be named in this model. In aerospace, supplier approval,
--   release status and certificates are controlled by the quality system; OTD is a logistics figure and does not release material.

title: Takt time versus actual cycle time per line in DAX with correct weighting over days
summary: DAX measures that compare takt time and actual cycle time per line using totals instead of averaged daily values, blank takt for mixed selections, a boundary-correct status and a count of lines slower than takt.
body:
-- ==== What it does ====
-- Compares takt time (the pace the customer demands) with the actual cycle time of each line, correctly weighted over days.
--   Takt time = available production time / customer demand (same period, same unit)
--   Actual cycle time = time the line spent producing / units produced
-- Both are ratios of sums, so a two-day view uses total time over total units and not the average of two daily values. Takt is only
-- meaningful for ONE line or one product flow, so it returns blank when several lines are in the selection (HASONEVALUE), and a
-- separate measure counts how many lines are slower than takt in the current selection. A status measure uses <= because a cycle
-- time equal to takt still meets demand.

-- ==== Required tables/columns (assumed star schema) ====
-- Fact: 'Fact Line Day'. GRAIN: one row per production line and calendar day. Columns: Date, LineKey, AvailableSeconds (planned production
--   time of the day minus breaks and planned stops, in seconds), DemandUnits (customer demand the line must serve that day, in units),
--   UnitsProduced (good units made), ProducingSeconds (time the line was actually making units, excluding stops).
-- Dimensions: 'Dim Date' (Date; marked as date table), 'Dim Line' (LineKey, Line, Plant, Product Family).
-- RELATIONSHIPS: 'Dim Date'[Date] -> 'Fact Line Day'[Date]; 'Dim Line'[LineKey] -> 'Fact Line Day'[LineKey]; both one-to-many, single direction.
-- If one line makes several products with different cycle times, add ProductKey to the grain and compare per product; one takt per mixed
--   line is not meaningful.

-- ==== Code ====
Available Seconds =
SUM ( 'Fact Line Day'[AvailableSeconds] )

Demand Units =
SUM ( 'Fact Line Day'[DemandUnits] )

Units Produced =
SUM ( 'Fact Line Day'[UnitsProduced] )

Producing Seconds =
SUM ( 'Fact Line Day'[ProducingSeconds] )

-- Takt only for a single line in scope; blank for several lines, because adding up available time of lines that make different
-- products and dividing by their demand mixes unlike things.
Takt Time (s) =
IF ( HASONEVALUE ( 'Dim Line'[Line] ), DIVIDE ( [Available Seconds], [Demand Units] ) )

Cycle Time (s) =
IF ( HASONEVALUE ( 'Dim Line'[Line] ), DIVIDE ( [Producing Seconds], [Units Produced] ) )

-- Above 1.0: the line is slower than demand requires
Cycle to Takt Ratio =
DIVIDE ( [Cycle Time (s)], [Takt Time (s)] )

-- Units per hour the customer demand requires, and what the line actually delivers while producing
Required Units per Hour =
DIVIDE ( 3600, [Takt Time (s)] )

Line Capacity Units per Hour =
DIVIDE ( 3600, [Cycle Time (s)] )

Takt Status =
VAR Cycle = [Cycle Time (s)]
VAR Takt  = [Takt Time (s)]
RETURN
    IF ( ISBLANK ( Cycle ) || ISBLANK ( Takt ), BLANK (), IF ( ROUND ( Cycle, 2 ) <= ROUND ( Takt, 2 ), "Meets takt", "Slower than takt" ) )

-- Works for any selection: counts lines whose own cycle time is above their own takt. [Cycle Time (s)] and [Takt Time (s)]
-- are evaluated per line because the row context of VALUES turns into a filter on the line.
Lines Slower than Takt =
COUNTROWS (
    FILTER ( VALUES ( 'Dim Line'[Line] ), [Cycle Time (s)] > [Takt Time (s)] )
)

-- Share of the day's available time the line would need to meet demand at its measured cycle time (above 100 percent = not enough time)
Required Time Utilisation =
DIVIDE ( [Demand Units] * [Cycle Time (s)], [Available Seconds] )

-- ==== Worked example (invented numbers, verified by calculation) ====
-- Two days, two lines. Available time 27000 s per line and day (7.5 hours).
--   Line 1: day 1 demand 450, produced 450, producing 24300 s;  day 2 demand 300, produced 300, producing 18000 s
--   Line 2: day 1 demand 400, produced 380, producing 27000 s;  day 2 demand 380, produced 340, producing 27000 s
-- Line 1: takt = 54000 / 750 = 72.00 s. Daily takt would be 60.0 s and 90.0 s; their plain average is 75.0 s, which is wrong because the days carry different demand.
--   Cycle time = 42300 / 750 = 56.40 s (daily 54.0 s and 60.0 s; the plain average 57.0 s is wrong as well). Ratio 0.783: meets takt.
-- Line 2: takt = 54000 / 780 = 69.23 s. Cycle time = 54000 / 720 = 75.00 s. Ratio 1.083: slower than takt. Capacity 48.0 units/h against 52.0 required.
--   Required time utilisation = 780 x 75.00 / 54000 = 108.3%: the demand would need more than the available time.
-- Total row (both lines in scope): Takt Time and Cycle Time are blank; Lines Slower than Takt = 1.
-- Status uses <=: if a line's cycle time equals its takt exactly it meets takt.

-- ==== How to adapt ====
-- Demand in your planning system may be weekly: aggregate to the day in the source or keep the grain and make sure available time uses the same period.
-- If your takt definition subtracts breaks and meetings, do that in AvailableSeconds in the source and document it.
-- Use cycle time from time studies or machine data for ProducingSeconds; if the line has several stations, the cycle time of the whole line
--   is determined by the slowest station (bottleneck), so keep station cycle times in a separate fact.
-- Add a product dimension if lines change over: the same logic works per product, and the line total then becomes blank by design.
-- Reduce to a card for one line: put Line in a slicer; HASONEVALUE is then true and the measures show.

-- ==== Performance notes ====
-- One fact, simple sums; the FILTER over VALUES ( Line ) iterates the number of lines, a handful.

-- ==== Common mistakes ====
-- Averaging daily takt or cycle values instead of dividing the summed times by the summed demand and units.
-- Showing one takt for several lines in one total row.
-- Mixing units: demand in pieces, production in kits.
-- Using produced units (including scrap) for cycle time while demand is in good units; say which one you use.
-- Using < instead of <= in the status: a line exactly at takt then looks like a gap.
-- Treating cycle time as equal to takt when the line is simply forced to wait; waiting is a loss, not the pace.

-- ==== Privacy and safety ====
-- Line and demand data are business data, no personal data. Do not add operator names to this dataset; discuss with the works council how
--   line results may be used. Cycle times are planning figures and do not replace work instructions or approved process data.

title: Inventory turnover and days of inventory in DAX from month-end snapshots
summary: DAX measures for annualised inventory turns and days of inventory that treat stock as semi-additive: closing balance with LASTNONBLANK, average of month-end values and days limited to the data, with a checked example.
body:
-- ==== What it does ====
-- Inventory turnover and days of inventory on a model with a month-end snapshot fact and a consumption fact.
--   Turns (annualised) = consumption value of the period / average inventory value x 365 / days in the period
--   Days of inventory = average inventory value / consumption value x days in the period
-- Stock is a semi-additive quantity: it can be added across parts but never across dates. The closing balance of a period is the
-- snapshot of its last date with data, and the average inventory is the average of the month-end balances in the period. Summing
-- the snapshot rows over a quarter would triple-count the stock.

-- ==== Required tables/columns (assumed star schema) ====
-- Fact 1: 'Fact Inventory Snapshot'. GRAIN: one row per part and month-end snapshot date. Columns: SnapshotDate, PartKey, QtyOnHand, StockValue.
-- Fact 2: 'Fact Consumption'. GRAIN: one row per part and day. Columns: Date, PartKey, ConsumedValue (value of material issued to
--   production, or cost of goods sold, as defined in your finance policy).
-- Dimensions: 'Dim Date' (Date, Year, MonthNumber, YearMonth text such as 2026-01; contiguous, one row per calendar day, marked as date table),
--   'Dim Part' (PartKey, PartNumber, Category, ABCClass).
-- RELATIONSHIPS, one-to-many, single direction: 'Dim Date'[Date] -> 'Fact Inventory Snapshot'[SnapshotDate] and -> 'Fact Consumption'[Date];
--   'Dim Part'[PartKey] -> both facts.
-- The turnover figure only makes sense with a full-year view or a stated period; one month gives a very noisy value.

-- ==== Code ====
Consumption Value =
SUM ( 'Fact Consumption'[ConsumedValue] )

-- Last snapshot with data inside the current date selection (the balance at the end of the period).
-- LASTNONBLANK handles an incomplete current month, where the last calendar day has no snapshot yet.
Closing Inventory Value =
CALCULATE (
    SUM ( 'Fact Inventory Snapshot'[StockValue] ),
    LASTNONBLANK ( 'Dim Date'[Date], CALCULATE ( COUNTROWS ( 'Fact Inventory Snapshot' ) ) )
)

-- Average of the month-end balances of the months in the selection; months without a snapshot are skipped by AVERAGEX
Average Inventory Value =
AVERAGEX ( VALUES ( 'Dim Date'[YearMonth] ), [Closing Inventory Value] )

-- Last day with consumption data, ignoring every filter; REMOVEFILTERS () keeps part and date filters from changing it.
Last Consumption Date =
CALCULATE ( MAX ( 'Fact Consumption'[Date] ), REMOVEFILTERS () )

-- Days of the selection up to the last day with data, so a year in progress is not diluted by future days
Days in Period =
VAR LastData = [Last Consumption Date]
RETURN
    COUNTROWS ( FILTER ( VALUES ( 'Dim Date'[Date] ), 'Dim Date'[Date] <= LastData ) )

Inventory Turns (annualised) =
DIVIDE ( [Consumption Value], [Average Inventory Value] ) * DIVIDE ( 365, [Days in Period] )

Days of Inventory =
DIVIDE ( [Average Inventory Value], [Consumption Value] ) * [Days in Period]

-- Turns rank across part categories; blank on the total row
Turns Rank (category) =
IF (
    ISINSCOPE ( 'Dim Part'[Category] ),
    RANKX ( ALLSELECTED ( 'Dim Part'[Category] ), [Inventory Turns (annualised)], , DESC, Dense )
)

-- ==== Worked example (invented numbers, verified by calculation) ====
-- January to March 2026 = 90 days. Month-end stock value and consumption value per part:
--   P1: stock [50000, 46000, 54000], consumption [30000, 28000, 31000]
--   P2: stock [20000, 24000, 22000], consumption [6000, 5000, 7000]
-- P1: average inventory = (50000 + 46000 + 54000) / 3 = 50000; consumption 89000; turns = 89000 / 50000 x 365 / 90 = 7.219; days of inventory = 50.6.
-- P2: average inventory = 22000; consumption 18000; turns = 3.318; days of inventory = 110.0.
-- Both parts (total row): month-end totals are 70000, 70000, 76000; average inventory 72000; consumption 107000; turns = 6.027; days of inventory = 60.6.
-- The wrong way: summing the three snapshots (216000) as 'inventory' would give turns of 2.009, three times too low.
-- If the report is opened on 15 April and consumption data ends on 31 March, Last Consumption Date stays 31 March and Days in Period for a
--   'year 2026' selection is 90, not 365.

-- ==== How to adapt ====
-- Quarter or year: the same measures work; with more months the average inventory becomes more stable. Use at least twelve months for a yearly figure.
-- Quantity based turns: build the same pair with QtyOnHand and consumed quantity when parts are comparable in units.
-- Weekly snapshots: replace the YearMonth grouping column in Average Inventory Value by a week column of the date table.
-- Slow movers and obsolescence: add a measure for stock value of parts with no consumption in the last twelve months, defined in your inventory policy.
-- Aerospace spares: low turns can be intended (safety stock for rarely used rotables); use ABCClass or a criticality column on 'Dim Part' to compare like with like.

-- ==== Performance notes ====
-- AVERAGEX iterates months, not days; with a few years of data that is dozens of iterations, each with two small aggregations.
-- The snapshot table grows with parts times months; that is far smaller than a daily stock history.

-- ==== Common mistakes ====
-- Adding snapshot values across dates (a plain SUM over a quarter). Stock must be taken at a point in time and averaged.
-- Using LASTDATE instead of LASTNONBLANK and getting blank for the current month because the last calendar day has no snapshot yet.
-- Dividing by 365 days for a year in progress; use the days that have data.
-- Mixing consumption at cost with stock at a different valuation (standard cost vs moving average).
-- ALL ( 'Dim Date' ) in the last-date measure: it clears only the date filters, so a part filter still changes the result and every part gets its own last date.
--   REMOVEFILTERS () clears every filter, which is what 'last day with data in the whole model' means.
-- Reading a turns rank of one category without checking that the categories hold comparable parts.

-- ==== Privacy and safety ====
-- Inventory and consumption values are business data without personal data. Stock valuations can be commercially sensitive; limit the dataset to the roles that need it.
-- In aerospace, serialised and shelf-life parts have traceability and release rules in the quality system; this model is a planning figure and
--   does not replace stores records or part traceability.

title: Downtime Pareto with a correct cumulative percentage line in DAX using ALLSELECTED and ISINSCOPE
summary: DAX measures for a downtime Pareto: ranked reasons, cumulative minutes with a tie-break, cumulative percent that follows slicers, blank totals via ISINSCOPE and a vital-few class with a clear 80 percent boundary rule.
body:
-- ==== What it does ====
-- A downtime Pareto with a correct cumulative percentage line. For every reason it adds up the minutes of all reasons that rank higher,
-- with a tie-break so that reasons with equal minutes get a stable order, and divides by the total of the current selection. The measures
-- return blank on subtotal and total rows (ISINSCOPE), because a cumulative value has no meaning there. ALLSELECTED on the reason column
-- ignores the rows of the visual but keeps slicers (machine, line, date, reason category), so the Pareto always describes the selection the user made.
-- A class measure marks the 'vital few' reasons: reasons that start below 80 percent of cumulative downtime, which includes the reason that crosses the 80 percent line.

-- ==== Required tables/columns (assumed star schema) ====
-- Fact: 'Fact Downtime'. GRAIN: one row per downtime event. Columns: EventID, Date (start date), MachineKey, ReasonKey, Minutes.
-- Dimensions: 'Dim Date' (Date; marked as date table), 'Dim Machine' (MachineKey, Machine, Line, Plant), 'Dim Downtime Reason'
--   (ReasonKey, Reason, Category). Reason must be unique per row of the dimension.
-- RELATIONSHIPS, one-to-many, single direction: each dimension to 'Fact Downtime'.
-- Visual: a combo chart with the reason on the axis, [Downtime Min] as columns and [Downtime Cumulative %] as a line on a secondary axis (0 to 100 percent),
--   sorted by [Downtime Min] descending. The sort of the visual is not done by DAX; set it in the visual. Equal values are ordered by name in the measure;
--   in the visual add a second sort by Reason ascending for the same order.

-- ==== Code ====
Downtime Min =
SUM ( 'Fact Downtime'[Minutes] )

-- Total of the visual: all reasons that are visible after slicers, regardless of the row of the visual
Downtime Total (selection) =
CALCULATE ( [Downtime Min], ALLSELECTED ( 'Dim Downtime Reason' ) )

-- Minutes of this reason plus all reasons that rank above it. Rank order: more minutes first, equal minutes by name A to Z.
Downtime Cumulative Min =
VAR CurrentReason = SELECTEDVALUE ( 'Dim Downtime Reason'[Reason] )
VAR CurrentMin    = [Downtime Min]
VAR Reasons =
    ADDCOLUMNS ( ALLSELECTED ( 'Dim Downtime Reason'[Reason] ), "@Min", [Downtime Min] )
RETURN
    IF (
        ISINSCOPE ( 'Dim Downtime Reason'[Reason] ),
        SUMX (
            FILTER (
                Reasons,
                [@Min] > CurrentMin
                    || ( [@Min] = CurrentMin && 'Dim Downtime Reason'[Reason] <= CurrentReason )
            ),
            [@Min]
        )
    )

Downtime Cumulative % =
DIVIDE ( [Downtime Cumulative Min], [Downtime Total (selection)] )

-- Rank 1 = largest loss; reasons with equal minutes share a rank (Dense). Blank on subtotals.
Downtime Rank =
IF (
    ISINSCOPE ( 'Dim Downtime Reason'[Reason] ),
    RANKX ( ALLSELECTED ( 'Dim Downtime Reason'[Reason] ), [Downtime Min], , DESC, Dense )
)

-- Class A = vital few. A reason is in class A when the cumulative share BEFORE it is below 80 percent (strictly), so that
-- the reason that carries the total across 80 percent is still included.
Downtime Pareto Class =
VAR ShareBefore =
    DIVIDE ( [Downtime Cumulative Min] - [Downtime Min], [Downtime Total (selection)] )
RETURN
    IF ( ISINSCOPE ( 'Dim Downtime Reason'[Reason] ) && NOT ISBLANK ( ShareBefore ), IF ( ShareBefore < 0.8, "A", "B/C" ) )

-- ==== Worked example (invented minutes, verified by calculation) ====
-- One month, all machines selected, total 1200 minutes. Sorted by minutes descending, ties by name:
--   Material shortage  Min=420  Cumulative min= 420  Cumulative %= 35.0%  Cum % before this reason=  0.0%  Class=A
--   Spindle fault      Min=310  Cumulative min= 730  Cumulative %= 60.8%  Cum % before this reason= 35.0%  Class=A
--   Operator absent    Min=180  Cumulative min= 910  Cumulative %= 75.8%  Cum % before this reason= 60.8%  Class=A
--   Tool change        Min=180  Cumulative min=1090  Cumulative %= 90.8%  Cum % before this reason= 75.8%  Class=A
--   Waiting for QA     Min= 90  Cumulative min=1180  Cumulative %= 98.3%  Cum % before this reason= 90.8%  Class=B/C
--   Other              Min= 20  Cumulative min=1200  Cumulative %=100.0%  Cum % before this reason= 98.3%  Class=B/C
-- Operator absent and Tool change both have 180 minutes. Without a tie-break both rows would get the same cumulative value, the line would show
--   a flat step and one of the two percentages would be wrong; with the name rule Operator absent comes first (cumulative 910) and Tool change second (1090).
-- Tool change starts at 75.8% (below 80 percent) and ends at 90.8%: it is class A because the share BEFORE it is below 80 percent.
--   Waiting for QA starts at 90.8% and is class B/C.
-- Downtime Rank: Material shortage 1, Spindle fault 2, Operator absent 3, Tool change 3, Waiting for QA 4, Other 5.
-- The total row of the visual shows blank for Cumulative Min, Cumulative %, Rank and Class; [Downtime Min] shows 1200.
-- Slicer check: select only the reason category 'Planned' in a slicer on Dim Downtime Reason and the Pareto is calculated over those reasons only,
--   because ALLSELECTED keeps the slicer; with a plain ALL on the reason table it would still include all reasons in the total.

-- ==== How to adapt ====
-- Group small reasons into 'Other': build the grouping in the dimension (a column ReasonGroup) and use that column in place of Reason in the measures.
-- Pareto by cost instead of minutes: replace [Downtime Min] by a cost measure everywhere; the structure stays the same.
-- Top N only: show rows where [Downtime Rank] <= 5 with a visual filter on the rank measure; the cumulative values are still computed over all visible reasons.
-- Change the 80 percent line to your own convention; the strict < at the boundary is a choice, write it into the definition.
-- Combine with a machine slicer to build a Pareto per machine; nothing in the measures is hard-coded to a machine.

-- ==== Performance notes ====
-- The measure iterates the reasons (dozens), and each iteration evaluates the base measure once; this is fast.
-- If you have hundreds of reasons, group them in the dimension first; a Pareto with 300 bars is not readable anyway.

-- ==== Common mistakes ====
-- Using ALL ( 'Dim Downtime Reason' ) to build the list of reasons: slicers on category are then ignored and the cumulative line does not reach 100 percent.
-- Forgetting the tie-break: reasons with equal minutes then get the same cumulative value or are skipped.
-- No ISINSCOPE guard: the total row shows a cumulative value that equals the grand total or a meaningless figure.
-- Putting the cumulative line on the same axis as the minutes; it must use a percent axis from 0 to 100.
-- Using <= 80 percent for the class so that the crossing reason falls out of the vital few, or using the cumulative share after the reason instead of before.
-- Sorting the visual by reason name: the cumulative values are correct but the chart is not a Pareto.

-- ==== Privacy and safety ====
-- Downtime reasons are machine data. If operators select the reason, do not show results per operator; discuss with the works council how reason data may be used.
-- The Pareto points to where to look; the decision about corrective action remains with the responsible people. In aerospace and MRO, it does not replace maintenance or quality records.

title: OEE Calculator in Excel with Weighted Line Roll-up (Availability, Performance, Quality)
summary: Excel log sheet and summary that calculate availability, performance, quality and OEE per shift, check for impossible values, and roll up per line with sums instead of averaging percentages.
body:
## What it does
Calculates OEE per shift from five inputs (planned minutes, downtime minutes, ideal cycle time, total parts, good parts), flags impossible data, and rolls up per line correctly. The roll-up uses sums, because averaging the OEE percentages of shifts with different planned times gives a wrong number. It works in every Excel version with SUMIFS (Excel 2007 and later). No dynamic arrays needed.

## Definitions used
- Run time = planned time minus downtime.
- Availability = run time / planned time.
- Ideal minutes = total parts x ideal cycle time (s) / 60.
- Performance = ideal minutes / run time.
- Quality = good parts / total parts.
- OEE = availability x performance x quality = (good parts x ideal cycle time / 60) / planned time.
Agree the definition of planned time and of the ideal cycle time in your plant before comparing lines. Document it on the sheet.

## Sheet OEE_Log (row 1 headers, data from row 2)
A Date, B Line, C Shift, D Planned min, E Downtime min, F Ideal cycle s, G Total parts, H Good parts. Calculated columns, entered in row 2 and filled down:

```
I2: =D2-E2
J2: =F2*G2/60
K2: =IF(D2>0,I2/D2,"")
L2: =IF(I2>0,J2/I2,"")
M2: =IF(G2>0,H2/G2,"")
N2: =IF(COUNT(K2:M2)=3,K2*L2*M2,"")
O2: =IF(H2>G2,"Good > total",IF(E2>D2,"Downtime > planned",IF(L2>1,"Performance > 100%: check ideal cycle","OK")))
```
Format K to N as percent. Column O is the data quality check. Performance above 100 percent almost always means the ideal cycle time is too slow or the part count includes something it should not.

## Sheet Summary (one row per line, lines typed in column A from row 2)
```
B2: =SUMIFS(OEE_Log!$D$2:$D$500,OEE_Log!$B$2:$B$500,$A2)
C2: =SUMIFS(OEE_Log!$I$2:$I$500,OEE_Log!$B$2:$B$500,$A2)
D2: =SUMIFS(OEE_Log!$J$2:$J$500,OEE_Log!$B$2:$B$500,$A2)
E2: =SUMIFS(OEE_Log!$G$2:$G$500,OEE_Log!$B$2:$B$500,$A2)
F2: =SUMIFS(OEE_Log!$H$2:$H$500,OEE_Log!$B$2:$B$500,$A2)
G2: =C2/B2
H2: =D2/C2
I2: =F2/E2
J2: =G2*H2*I2
K2: =AVERAGEIFS(OEE_Log!$N$2:$N$500,OEE_Log!$B$2:$B$500,$A2)
```
Headers for B to K: Planned min, Run min, Ideal min, Total, Good, Availability, Performance, Quality, OEE, Simple average (for comparison only). If your data will grow beyond row 500, convert the log to a Table (Ctrl+T) and use structured references or extend the ranges.

## Worked example (invented data, 2 March)
| Line | Shift | Planned | Down | Ideal s | Total | Good | Run | Ideal min | A | P | Q | OEE |
| L1 | Early | 450 | 54 | 40 | 480 | 456 | 396 | 320.0 | 88.0% | 80.8% | 95.0% | 67.6% |
| L1 | Late | 450 | 90 | 40 | 380 | 349 | 360 | 253.3 | 80.0% | 70.4% | 91.8% | 51.7% |
| L1 | Night | 240 | 20 | 40 | 320 | 312 | 220 | 213.3 | 91.7% | 97.0% | 97.5% | 86.7% |
| L2 | Early | 450 | 45 | 60 | 300 | 291 | 405 | 300.0 | 90.0% | 74.1% | 97.0% | 64.7% |
| L2 | Late | 450 | 120 | 60 | 210 | 195 | 330 | 210.0 | 73.3% | 63.6% | 92.9% | 43.3% |

Roll-up L1: planned 1,140, run 976, ideal 786.7, total 1,180, good 1,117. Availability 976 / 1,140 = 85.6 percent, performance 786.7 / 976 = 80.6 percent, quality 1,117 / 1,180 = 94.7 percent, OEE = 65.3 percent. Cross-check: 1,117 x 40 / 60 / 1,140 = 65.3 percent. The simple average of the three shift OEE values is 68.6 percent, 3.3 points too high, because the short night shift with its good result has the same weight as a full shift. L2 roll-up: 900 planned, 735 run, 510 ideal, 510 total, 486 good, A 81.7 percent, P 69.4 percent, Q 95.3 percent, OEE 54.0 percent.

## How to adapt
- Add a column for planned stops if you want to separate them from downtime.
- Add reason columns (breakdown, changeover, minor stops) and use the minutes-based loss view: every loss in minutes, as a share of planned time.
- Use conditional formatting on column N with thresholds that your plant sets. Do not copy a world-class value from the internet without agreeing it locally.
- For several machines per line, add a Machine column and a second SUMIFS criterion.

## Common mistakes
- Averaging percentages of unequal shifts (see example).
- Changing the ideal cycle time to improve the score. Keep one documented reference, for example the best demonstrated rate, and change it only with a note.
- Entering downtime in hours in one row and minutes in another.
- Counting parts that are reworked later as good parts, in some shifts and not in others.
- Text numbers: if a value is left-aligned and SUMIFS ignores it, convert it with Data > Text to Columns.

## Data protection and safety
The sheet contains machine and shift data. If shift names or operator names are added, remember that OEE by person is performance data of employees and needs the works council and data protection involved. Store the file in a SharePoint library with the right permissions, not on a USB stick. The numbers support improvement work; they are not a quality record for released parts.

title: Value Stream Table in Excel: Lead Time, Queue Days, Value-Added Ratio and Bottleneck
summary: Excel sheet for a current-state value stream: takt, queue days from WIP, lead time, value-added ratio and the bottleneck step by effective cycle time, using only classic functions.
body:
## What it does
Holds the numbers behind a current-state value stream map and calculates takt time, effective cycle time per step, queue time in days, total lead time, value-added ratio and the bottleneck. It makes the typical finding visible: lead time is mostly waiting, not working. It uses only SUM, MAX, INDEX and MATCH, so it works in any Excel version.

## Layout (sheet VSM)
Inputs at the top:
```
A1: Demand per day (pcs)           B1: 200
A2: Available time per day (s)     B2: 27000
A3: Takt time (s)                  B3: =B2/B1
```
Step table, headers in row 5, steps in rows 6 to 10 (add rows and extend the ranges for more steps). Columns A to E are typed: Step, Cycle time s, Value-adding (Y or N), Uptime (fraction), WIP before step (pieces). Columns F to H are formulas:
```
F6: =B6/D6            effective cycle time
G6: =E6/$B$1          queue days (WIP divided by daily demand)
H6: =IF(C6="Y",B6,0)  value-adding seconds
```
Fill F6:H6 down. Results below the table:
```
B12: =SUM(B6:B10)                       total processing time (s)
B13: =SUM(G6:G10)                       total queue (days)
B14: =B13+B12/B2                        lead time (working days)
B15: =SUM(H6:H10)                       value-adding time (s)
B16: =B15/(B14*B2)                      value-added ratio
B17: =INDEX(A6:A10,MATCH(MAX(F6:F10),F6:F10,0))   bottleneck step
B18: =MAX(F6:F10)                       bottleneck effective CT (s)
B19: =B18/B3                            bottleneck load vs takt
```
Format B16 and B19 as percent with two decimals (B16 is tiny).

## Worked example (invented data)
Demand 200 pieces per day, 27,000 s available, takt = 135 s.
| Step | CT s | VA | Uptime | WIP | Effective CT | Queue days |
| Cut | 38 | Y | 90% | 800 | 42.2 | 4.0 |
| Drill | 52 | Y | 95% | 600 | 54.7 | 3.0 |
| Deburr | 45 | N | 92% | 400 | 48.9 | 2.0 |
| Inspect | 30 | N | 100% | 200 | 30.0 | 1.0 |
| Pack | 20 | N | 100% | 100 | 20.0 | 0.5 |

Processing time 185 s. Queue 10.5 days. Lead time = 10.5 + 185 / 27,000 = 10.507 days. Value-adding time 90 s (Cut and Drill), so value-added ratio = 90 / (10.507 x 27,000) = 0.032 percent. Bottleneck: Drill at 54.7 s, which is 40.6 percent of takt. Reading: capacity is no problem, the process waits. Reducing WIP before each step to 100 pieces (half a day of demand, an assumption) would cut queue to 2.5 days.

## How to adapt
- Batch processes: add a batch size column and use cycle time per piece = batch time / batch size.
- Changeover: add a changeover column and divide it by the lot size to get the contribution per piece.
- Steps in parallel: enter the combined cycle time (cycle time divided by the number of identical machines) if they share one queue.
- Future state: copy the sheet, change WIP and uptime, and compare lead time in a small table.

## Common mistakes
- Queue days from WIP divided by daily output instead of daily demand. If the line is behind, output differs from demand; choose one and say which.
- Uptime entered as 90 instead of 0.9 (cycle time is then divided by 90).
- Marking inspection or documentation as value-adding. Required, but not value-adding.
- Reading the value-added ratio as precise. It is an order of magnitude; the point is the difference between waiting and working.
- Mixing working days and calendar days in the lead time. Use working days and state it.

## Data protection and safety
The data are process data. Do not publish customer-confidential part numbers in a shared workbook outside the people who need them. A value stream table supports a workshop; any change to a regulated process (for example in aircraft production or maintenance) still goes through the normal change control and quality approval.

title: SMED Changeover Sheet in Excel: Internal vs External Time, Savings and Freed Capacity
summary: Excel sheet for a SMED study: classify each changeover element as internal or external before and after, and calculate machine downtime saved, percent reduction and freed capacity per week.
body:
## What it does
SMED means reducing changeover time by separating internal elements (done while the machine is stopped) from external ones (done while it runs) and then shortening both. This sheet lists each element of a changeover, records its type and duration now and in the proposed state, and calculates how much stopped time is saved. It uses SUMIFS and COUNTIFS (Excel 2007 and later). One optional formula needs Excel 2021 or Microsoft 365.

## Layout (sheet SMED)
Row 1 headers: A #, B Element, C Current type, D Current s, E Proposed type, F Proposed s. Elements from row 2 to row 11 (extend as needed). Types are typed as Internal or External. Add a drop-down: select C2:C11 and E2:E11, Data > Data Validation > List, source: Internal,External. This avoids typos that SUMIFS would silently ignore.

Parameters and results in columns H and I:
```
I1: 6                                           changeovers per week
I2: 40                                          cycle time (s per part)
I4: =SUMIFS(D2:D11,C2:C11,"Internal")           internal time now (s)
I5: =SUMIFS(F2:F11,E2:E11,"Internal")           internal time proposed (s)
I6: =I4-I5                                      reduction (s)
I7: =IF(I4>0,I6/I4,0)                           reduction (%)
I8: =COUNTIFS(C2:C11,"Internal",E2:E11,"External")   elements moved to external
I9: =SUMIFS(D2:D11,C2:C11,"Internal",E2:E11,"External")   seconds moved to external
I10: =I6*I1/60                                  machine minutes freed per week
I11: =I6*I1/I2                                  extra parts per week (upper bound)
```
Optional list of moved elements (Excel 2021 or Microsoft 365, spills): `=FILTER(B2:B11,(C2:C11="Internal")*(E2:E11="External"),"none")`. In older versions use a filter on the table instead.

## Worked example (invented data, CNC changeover)
| # | Element | Now | s | Proposed | s |
| 1 | Fetch fixture from tool crib | Internal | 300 | External | 300 |
| 2 | Stop machine, clear chips | Internal | 120 | Internal | 90 |
| 3 | Remove old fixture | Internal | 240 | Internal | 150 |
| 4 | Clean machine table | Internal | 180 | Internal | 120 |
| 5 | Stage new program and NC data | Internal | 150 | External | 150 |
| 6 | Mount new fixture | Internal | 420 | Internal | 240 |
| 7 | Set work offsets (touch-off) | Internal | 360 | Internal | 180 |
| 8 | Load program, dry run | Internal | 300 | Internal | 180 |
| 9 | First-off inspection | Internal | 600 | Internal | 540 |
| 10 | Prepare job documents | Internal | 180 | External | 180 |

Results: internal time now = 2,850 s (47.5 min). Proposed internal time = 90 + 150 + 120 + 240 + 180 + 180 + 540 = 1,500 s (25 min). Reduction 1,350 s = 47.4 percent. Three elements move to external, 630 s (300 + 150 + 180). With 6 changeovers per week: 1,350 x 6 / 60 = 135 machine minutes freed. At 40 s per part this is at most 1,350 x 6 / 40 = 202.5 additional parts per week, an upper bound that assumes the machine has demand and material for them.

## How to adapt
- Record the real durations from a video of one changeover, not from memory. Time each element once, then average several changeovers.
- Add a column Owner (role) and one for the improvement idea per element.
- Add a changeover cost: freed minutes times your machine hour rate, if finance agrees on the rate.
- Keep the same sheet per machine family; do not mix different changeover types in one list.

## Common mistakes
- Moving an element to External without anyone available to do it while the machine runs. The time does not disappear, the operator just does it later.
- Typing "internal" in one cell and "Internal " (trailing space) in another. Use the drop-down.
- Cutting inspection or release steps to reach a number. In regulated production, first-off or first-article checks stay; the quality function decides what can be prepared in advance. In aircraft maintenance, tool and torque checks follow approved procedures and are not SMED candidates.
- Reading the extra-parts figure as a promise.
- Adding the durations of external elements to the downtime. Only internal ones stop the machine.

## Data protection and safety
The sheet holds process data. If the changeover video shows people, check consent and works council agreements before storing or sharing it. Safety steps (lock-out, guards) are never shortened or reordered by a spreadsheet; the safety officer reviews any change to the changeover sequence.

title: Takt Time and Line Balancing Sheet in Excel with Station Load and Balance Efficiency
summary: Excel sheet that calculates takt time from shift data and yield, sums task times per station, flags stations over takt, and shows minimum stations and balance efficiency before and after a rebalance.
body:
## What it does
Calculates takt time from your shift pattern and demand, adds up task times per station, shows each station's utilisation of takt, flags stations that cannot keep up, and gives the minimum number of stations and the balance efficiency. It uses SUMIFS, ROUNDUP, MAX and COUNTIF, so it works in every Excel version since 2007.

## Layout (sheet Takt)
Inputs in A1:B6:
```
B1: 480     shift length (min)
B2: 45      breaks per shift (min)
B3: 15      huddle and cleaning per shift (min)
B4: 2       shifts per day
B5: 360     good units required per day
B6: 0.975   expected yield (fraction)
B8:  =(B1-B2-B3)*B4*60     net available time per day (s)
B9:  =B5/B6                units to start per day
B10: =B8/B9                takt time (s)
```
Task list in D1:F11 (headers Task, Time s, Station), one row per task with the station it is assigned to. Station table in H1:K5 for stations 1 to 4 (extend for more):
```
I2: =SUMIFS($E$2:$E$11,$F$2:$F$11,H2)      station load (s)
J2: =I2/$B$10                               utilisation of takt
K2: =IF(I2>$B$10,"Over takt","OK")
```
Fill down to row 5. Summary:
```
B12: =SUM(E2:E11)                total task time (s)
B13: =ROUNDUP(B12/B10,0)         minimum number of stations
B14: =COUNT(H2:H5)               stations used
B15: =MAX(I2:I5)                 slowest station load (s)
B16: =B12/(B14*B15)              balance efficiency
B17: =1-B16                      balance loss
B18: =COUNTIF(K2:K5,"Over takt") stations over takt
```

## Worked example (invented data)
Net available time = (480 - 45 - 15) x 2 x 60 = 50,400 s. Good units 360 at yield 97.5 percent means 360 / 0.975 = 369.2 units to start. Takt = 50,400 / 369.23 = 136.5 s.

Tasks (s): T1 22, T2 36, T3 30, T4 30, T5 44, T6 52, T7 44, T8 40, T9 62, T10 70. Assignment A: station 1 gets T1 to T4, station 2 gets T5 to T7, station 3 gets T8 and T9, station 4 gets T10.
| Station | Load s | Utilisation of takt | Flag |
| 1 | 118 | 86.4% | OK |
| 2 | 140 | 102.6% | Over takt |
| 3 | 102 | 74.7% | OK |
| 4 | 70 | 51.3% | OK |

Total task time 430 s, 430 / 136.5 = 3.15, so the minimum is 4 stations. Balance efficiency = 430 / (4 x 140) = 76.8 percent, balance loss 23.2 percent, one station over takt.

Rebalance: move T7 (44 s) from station 2 to station 4, assuming the task sequence allows it. Loads become 118, 96, 102 and 114 s. Slowest 118 s, efficiency = 430 / (4 x 118) = 91.1 percent, no station over takt. Change cell F8 from 2 to 4 and the sheet shows it at once.

## How to adapt
- Different shift patterns: put each pattern in its own column and calculate takt per pattern.
- Add a column for the predecessor of each task and check by eye or with a second column that no task sits at an earlier station than its predecessor.
- Add a buffer target, for example plan stations at 90 percent of takt, as an input cell that replaces $B$10 in the flag formula, if your plant uses such a rule.
- For mixed models, use a weighted average task time per station from the product mix.

## Common mistakes
- Using gross shift time instead of net available time. Breaks and planned stops belong out of the denominator.
- Taking takt equal to cycle time. Takt is demand-driven; cycle time is what the process delivers.
- Forgetting yield, so the line is planned for good units but has to start more.
- Balancing to 100 percent of takt without any allowance for disturbance.
- Moving tasks without checking sequence, tools, ergonomics and qualifications. In aircraft assembly and maintenance, task order is often fixed by approved documents, and who may do a task is fixed by authorisation; the sheet cannot decide that.

## Data protection and safety
The sheet contains time data per task, not per person. Do not add operator names to station loads: station times used for individual assessment are performance data and need works council involvement. Ergonomic and safety limits stay with the responsible specialists.

title: 5S Scorecard in Excel with Area Matrix, Weights and Latest Audit per Area
summary: Excel workbook that stores 5S audit answers as rows, calculates percent per S and per area for a chosen audit date with optional weights, and finds the latest audit date per area.
body:
## What it does
Stores each audit answer as one row (date, area, S, question, score 0 to 4) and builds a matrix of areas by S for a chosen audit date. Because the scores are rows, you can add or remove questions without breaking formulas, and each S is divided by its own number of questions. It uses SUMIFS, COUNTIFS and SUMPRODUCT (Excel 2007 and later). The latest-audit column uses MAXIFS, which needs Excel 2019 or Microsoft 365.

## Sheet Answers (row 1 headers)
A Date, B Area, C S, D Question, E Score. The S column must contain exactly the names used in the matrix headers: Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardise, Sustain. Add data validation for E (Data > Data Validation > Whole number between 0 and 4) and a list for C. Scale used here: 0 = not in place, 2 = partly, 4 = in place and held; define your own wording in the audit instructions.

## Sheet Matrix
```
A1: Audit date    B1: 2026-03-09   (a real date)
Row 3 headers: A3 Area, B3 Sort, C3 Set in order, D3 Shine, E3 Standardise, F3 Sustain, G3 Weighted total, H3 Latest audit
Row 4: A4 Weight, B4 1, C4 1, D4 1, E4 2, F4 2          (weights are an example, set your own)
A5: Machining cell 1     A6: Assembly bay 2

B5: =IFERROR(SUMIFS(Answers!$E$2:$E$1000,Answers!$B$2:$B$1000,$A5,Answers!$C$2:$C$1000,B$3,Answers!$A$2:$A$1000,$B$1)/(4*COUNTIFS(Answers!$B$2:$B$1000,$A5,Answers!$C$2:$C$1000,B$3,Answers!$A$2:$A$1000,$B$1)),"")
G5: =IFERROR(SUMPRODUCT(B5:F5,$B$4:$F$4)/SUM($B$4:$F$4),"")
H5: =MAXIFS(Answers!$A$2:$A$1000,Answers!$B$2:$B$1000,$A5)
```
Fill B5 across to F5, then rows 5 to 6 down (and further for more areas). Format B to G as percent and H as date. If an S was not scored the cell shows empty, and SUMPRODUCT then treats it as zero, so for partial audits compare only complete audits. For equal weights set B4:F4 to 1.

## Worked example (invented data, audit of 9 March 2026)
Three questions per S. Machining cell 1: Sort 3, 4, 3; Set in order 2, 3, 3; Shine 4, 3, 3; Standardise 2, 2, 1; Sustain 1, 2, 2. Assembly bay 2: Sort 4, 4, 3; Set in order 3, 4, 4; Shine 3, 3, 4; Standardise 3, 3, 2; Sustain 2, 3, 3.

| Area | Sort | Set | Shine | Standardise | Sustain | Weighted | Plain average |
| Machining cell 1 | 83.3% | 66.7% | 83.3% | 41.7% | 41.7% | 57.1% | 63.3% |
| Assembly bay 2 | 91.7% | 91.7% | 83.3% | 66.7% | 66.7% | 76.2% | 80.0% |

Example: Sort for machining cell 1 = (3 + 4 + 3) / (4 x 3) = 10 / 12 = 83.3 percent. Weighted total = (83.3 + 66.7 + 83.3 + 2 x 41.7 + 2 x 41.7) / 7 = 57.1 percent. The weighting by 2 for Standardise and Sustain pulls the score down because those two are weak, which is the point: they decide whether the result lasts.

## How to adapt
- Conditional formatting (Home > Conditional Formatting > Color Scales or Highlight Cells) with thresholds that your plant sets. The thresholds are your decision.
- Trend: add the audit date as a row label and use several dates in column A of Answers; change B1 to compare.
- Add a Comments column with the evidence, for example a photo reference.
- Use a Microsoft Form or Lists form to collect answers and let Power Automate append them to the Answers table.

## Common mistakes
- Dates stored as text, so the date criterion matches nothing. Check with ISNUMBER.
- S names spelled differently in Answers and in the header cells (for example Set-in-order).
- Changing the weights after the first audits without noting it. History becomes incomparable.
- Treating the percentage as a goal in itself. The audit is there to find actions.
- Using the 5S score as a substitute for tool control, FOD checks, calibration status or safety inspections. In aviation maintenance those follow their own procedures and records.

## Data protection and safety
Answers can contain names in the comment field; use roles. Scores for an area are not scores for a person. Keep the workbook where only the audit team and area leads can edit, and check with the works council how audit results are used.

title: FMEA Sheet in Excel with RPN, Tie-Break Ranking, Review Flags and Before/After Comparison
summary: Excel FMEA worksheet that calculates RPN from severity, occurrence and detection, ranks failure modes without ties, flags rows for review by severity or RPN, and compares RPN before and after actions.
body:
## What it does
A working FMEA sheet for process or design failure modes. It calculates RPN = severity x occurrence x detection, ranks the failure modes with a tie-break so that every row has a unique rank, flags rows for review using two thresholds you set, and compares the RPN before and after actions. It uses RANK, COUNTIF, SUMIFS and INDEX/MATCH, so it works in all Excel versions since 2007. One optional formula needs Excel 2021 or Microsoft 365.

## Important note on the method
RPN is the classic method. The AIAG and VDA FMEA handbook published in 2019 replaced the RPN with an Action Priority table for automotive customers. Check which method your customer, your quality system or your standard requires before you use RPN as a decision rule. RPN has known weaknesses: it is a product of ordinal ratings, different combinations give the same number, and a high-severity item with low RPN can be overlooked. That is why this sheet adds a severity flag next to the RPN.

## Layout (sheet FMEA, headers in row 1, rows 2 to 9 as example)
A ID, B Process step, C Failure mode, D Effect, E Cause, F S, G O, H D (ratings 1 to 10, with the scale of your company), I RPN, J Rank, K Flag, L Action, M S new, N O new, O D new, P RPN new.
```
I2: =F2*G2*H2
J2: =RANK(I2,I$2:I$9)+COUNTIF(I$2:I2,I2)-1
K2: =IF(OR(F2>=Settings!$B$1,I2>=Settings!$B$2),"Review","")
P2: =IF(COUNT(M2:O2)=3,M2*N2*O2,"")
```
Sheet Settings: B1 = severity review level, B2 = RPN review level. Both are your team's rules; the values below are only for the example. Results block (columns R and S):
```
S1: =SUMIFS(I2:I9,P2:P9,">0")     RPN of rows that have an action with new ratings
S2: =SUM(P2:P9)                   RPN after actions
S3: =1-S2/S1                      reduction
S4: =INDEX(C2:C9,MATCH(1,J2:J9,0))   failure mode with rank 1
S5: =COUNTIF(K2:K9,"Review")      rows to review
```
Optional sorted list (Excel 2021 or Microsoft 365): `=SORTBY(C2:C9,I2:I9,-1)` spills the failure modes in descending RPN order; ties keep their original order.

## Worked example (invented data, maintenance process)
Settings: severity level 9, RPN level 100. Ratings are examples and not a statement about any real operation.
| Step | Failure mode | S | O | D | RPN | Rank | Flag |
| Fastener torque | Wrong torque value used | 9 | 3 | 4 | 108 | 4 | Review |
| Tool control | Tool left in work area | 9 | 2 | 6 | 108 | 5 | Review |
| Calibration | Expired torque wrench used | 8 | 3 | 3 | 72 | 6 | |
| Stores | Wrong part number picked | 7 | 4 | 5 | 140 | 3 | Review |
| Work card | Step skipped | 8 | 3 | 6 | 144 | 2 | Review |
| Labelling | Label unreadable | 4 | 5 | 3 | 60 | 8 | |
| Handover | Incomplete shift handover | 6 | 5 | 6 | 180 | 1 | Review |
| Cleaning | Wrong solvent | 5 | 2 | 7 | 70 | 7 | |

Rows 1 and 2 have the same RPN of 108: RANK gives both 4, and the COUNTIF part adds 0 to the first and 1 to the second, so the ranks are 4 and 5. Five rows are flagged (two by severity 9, five by RPN of 100 or more, with overlap).

Actions with new ratings: torque card change 9, 2, 3 = 54; tool shadow board and count 9, 2, 2 = 36; barcode scan 7, 2, 2 = 28; sign-off per step 8, 2, 3 = 48; written handover template 6, 3, 3 = 54. RPN before for these five rows: 108 + 108 + 140 + 144 + 180 = 680. After: 54 + 36 + 28 + 48 + 54 = 220. Reduction = 1 - 220 / 680 = 67.6 percent. Note that severity stays 9 for the first two rows: actions that reduce occurrence or improve detection do not lower severity unless the design changes.

## How to adapt
- Insert rows inside the range (not below it) so the formulas extend.
- Put rating scales (what is a 3 for occurrence in your process) on a second sheet and link them with a note or a comment.
- Add columns for owner (role), due date and status.
- If your customer requires Action Priority, replace column I and K with a lookup table that returns the priority from S, O and D as defined in the handbook you are working with.

## Common mistakes
- Treating RPN as a measure of risk to compare across different FMEAs.
- Lowering a detection rating because a check exists on paper, without evidence that it works.
- Re-rating only the rows with actions and leaving old ratings in the comparison. The before and after sums use the same rows on purpose.
- Letting one person fill the sheet. An FMEA is a team product.
- In aviation, a sheet like this is an analysis aid. It does not replace maintenance data, work cards, the safety management system or required occurrence reporting, and certifying staff retain release responsibility.

## Data protection and safety
FMEA rows sometimes describe incidents with people involved. Describe the process, not the person. Store the file in a library with limited edit rights and version history, because the history is evidence of how the team reached its ratings.

title: Adaptive Card: shift handover form for maintenance with aircraft reference and nothing-to-report toggle
summary: Adaptive Card 1.5 form for a written shift handover per aircraft or work order with validated shift and reference, a nothing-to-report toggle, open work, defects and parts, and Submit and Cancel.
body:
A written handover per aircraft or work order is easier to audit than a talk at the door. This card collects the fields that trade sources name for a maintenance handover: completed work, open work, new or closed defects, open parts or material and general problems. It also lets the team say 'nothing to report', because silence is not information. The regulatory basis and the required content belong in your maintenance organisation exposition (MOE) and procedures; check the current regulation and your MOE before you add or remove fields. The card is a convenience for the input; the record is stored in your system (a SharePoint list or your MRO software), not in the chat.

## Card JSON

```json
{
  "type": "AdaptiveCard",
  "$schema": "http://adaptivecards.io/schemas/adaptive-card.json",
  "version": "1.5",
  "msteams": {
    "width": "Full"
  },
  "body": [
    {
      "type": "TextBlock",
      "text": "Shift handover",
      "wrap": true,
      "size": "Large",
      "weight": "Bolder"
    },
    {
      "type": "TextBlock",
      "text": "One card per aircraft or work order. 'Nothing to report' is also a handover.",
      "wrap": true,
      "isSubtle": true,
      "spacing": "None"
    },
    {
      "type": "Input.ChoiceSet",
      "id": "shift",
      "label": "Shift that ends",
      "isRequired": true,
      "errorMessage": "Select the shift",
      "style": "compact",
      "value": "late",
      "choices": [
        {
          "title": "Early",
          "value": "early"
        },
        {
          "title": "Late",
          "value": "late"
        },
        {
          "title": "Night",
          "value": "night"
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "type": "Input.Text",
      "id": "workRef",
      "label": "Aircraft registration or work order",
      "isRequired": true,
      "errorMessage": "Enter the aircraft or order",
      "placeholder": "Example: D-ABCD or WO-10442",
      "maxLength": 40
    },
    {
      "type": "Input.Toggle",
      "id": "nothing",
      "title": "Nothing to report for this aircraft or order",
      "valueOn": "yes",
      "valueOff": "no",
      "value": "no",
      "wrap": true
    },
    {
      "type": "Input.Text",
      "id": "done",
      "label": "Work completed",
      "isMultiline": true,
      "maxLength": 1000
    },
    {
      "type": "Input.Text",
      "id": "open",
      "label": "Work still open, including next step",
      "isMultiline": true,
      "maxLength": 1000
    },
    {
      "type": "Input.Text",
      "id": "defects",
      "label": "New or closed defects (reference numbers)",
      "isMultiline": true,
      "maxLength": 500
    },
    {
      "type": "Input.Text",
      "id": "parts",
      "label": "Parts or material open",
      "isMultiline": true,
      "maxLength": 500
    },
    {
      "type": "Input.Text",
      "id": "issues",
      "label": "General problems (tools, access, safety, documents)",
      "isMultiline": true,
      "maxLength": 500
    },
    {
      "type": "TextBlock",
      "text": "This card does not replace task cards, the technical log or certifying staff decisions.",
      "wrap": true,
      "isSubtle": true,
      "size": "Small"
    }
  ],
  "actions": [
    {
      "type": "Action.Submit",
      "title": "Submit handover",
      "data": {
        "form": "shiftHandover",
        "version": 1
      }
    },
    {
      "type": "Action.Submit",
      "title": "Cancel",
      "data": {
        "form": "cancel"
      },
      "associatedInputs": "none"
    }
  ]
}
```

## How to use

1. Post the card with Power Automate (Teams 'Post adaptive card and wait for a response', or in a channel with the card posting action) or from a bot. For a form that many people fill, a bot or a Teams message extension is better than a flow that waits.
2. When the user presses Submit, read the inputs by id: shift, workRef, nothing, done, open, defects, parts, issues. Write one row to the 'Shift Handovers' list with a ShiftKey built from the date and the shift. Use the same key as your reminder flow.
3. Server side checks that a card cannot do: if nothing is 'no', at least one of done, open, defects, parts or issues must be filled; the aircraft reference must exist in your fleet or work order list. Return the same card with a red line if the check fails.
4. The Cancel button uses associatedInputs none, so it works with empty required fields.

## Worked example (invented data)

Late shift, 21:50. The team lead selects 'Late', enters 'WO-10442' (invented), writes 'Left main gear inspection task cards 3 to 7 done', 'Task card 8 open, waiting for torque wrench from calibration, next shift continues at card 8', and 'Defect reference DEF-2231 opened, parts ordered'. Parts: 'One seal kit open'. Submit creates one row. A second aircraft on the same line without findings gets its own card with the toggle set to yes. The reminder flow later finds two rows for the shift key and sees no missing team.

## Common mistakes

- Making all text fields required. People then write 'n/a' in each; use the toggle for a true empty handover.
- Free text without limits. Set maxLength so the record stays readable and the card within the message size.
- Trusting the card to enforce content rules. It only checks required fields and patterns on the client.
- Keeping the record in chat. A chat message can be edited or lost; store a row.
- Using the card output as a release or certification statement. It is a handover note only.

## Teams rendering limits and compatibility

- Teams rendering (Microsoft Learn cards reference, read 20 Nov 2026): bots and action-based message extensions support schema 1.6 or earlier, and the Teams mobile app up to 1.6; newer versions may render inconsistently. This card declares 1.5 on purpose, so it stays inside what older clients show.
- Adaptive Cards are not supported in tabs or connectors, and file or image uploads are not supported inside cards. Images must be PNG, JPEG or GIF up to 1024 x 1024 pixels, hosted at a public address without redirects; SVG and animated GIF are not supported.
- Design guidance from the same source: set wrap to true on text, avoid horizontal scrolling, use at most three columns per ColumnSet, give an explicit pixel width to at most one column and keep it small. Teams mobile does not scroll sideways.
- A card can have up to six actions, but one to three primary actions read best. The Learn page also lists positive and destructive action styling as not supported in some contexts, so the button titles must carry the meaning (check what your clients show).
- The whole message, including the card, is limited to about 28 KB (Teams connector page); keep cards small.
- Input.Toggle and multi-line Input.Text render in Teams desktop, web and mobile. Check long forms on a phone: keep the number of inputs small so the user does not scroll through a wall of fields.
- isRequired and errorMessage need schema 1.3 or higher; the card uses 1.5.

## Adapt it

Add a ChoiceSet with the handing-over team, a field for tooling and test equipment in use, or a link to the work package. Translate the labels into the working language of the hangar; keep the ids stable.

## Privacy and security

Handover text can name employees, customers and aircraft. Do not post it into channels with guests. Apply the same access rules as for the technical records, and agree with the works council and data protection officer who may read handover history. Never paste manual text or task card content into the free text fields; reference the document and revision.
